title: Why App Blockers Don't Work for Some People (and What Helps Instead)

copy.cover_headline: Your blocker stops the app, not the wired feeling

points.headline: Blockers do cut minutes
points.body: In a 2023 field study, a delay app cut actual app opens by 57% over six weeks. Self-set limits reduced screen time too. For minutes, the research is encouraging.

points.headline: Mood is the weak spot
points.body: Two 2025 meta-analyses of social media breaks found a small well-being effect, or none at all. Cutting access changes minutes more reliably than it changes how you feel.

points.headline: The urge stays when access is cut
points.body: A blocker takes away the app, not the reason you reached for it. If you were restless or wanted relief, that need looks for another way out: the browser, another feed.

points.headline: Some people should keep a blocker
points.body: Want firm limits for work or sleep? Tap past pauses on autopilot? Have an app doing real harm? Then a hard blocker is still the right tool.

points.headline: A 30-second reset at the limit screen
points.body: Phone face down. One long sigh out. In through your nose for 4, out for 6, three rounds. Drop your shoulders. Then close the app or keep going, on purpose. Dizzy? Breathe normally.

reel_lines: You hit your limit, but the urge is still there.
The blocker took the app, not the wired feeling.
A longer exhale brings you back down.
copy.instagram_caption:
Your blocker can stop the app. It can't bring you down from the last scroll.

Next time the limit screen shows up, try this: put the phone face down and let out one long sigh. Then breathe in through your nose for 4 and out for 6. Three rounds, about 30 seconds.

Let your teeth part and your shoulders drop. Then decide on purpose: close the app, or keep going knowing you chose to.

Full guide: link in bio.

App blockers do cut minutes. In one 2023 study, a delay app cut app opens by 57% over six weeks. But research on social media breaks finds small or no effects on mood.

The blocker takes away the app. It doesn't touch the wound-up feeling that sent you there.

So at the limit screen, try 4 counts in, 6 out, three rounds. About 30 seconds.

copy.facebook_message:
Ever tapped "Ignore Limit" and felt a little worse afterward? That isn't a failure of self-control. Blockers manage minutes, but what often sends us back to the feed is how we feel: wound up, restless, wanting relief.

Blockers do work for cutting use, and if you want firm limits for work or sleep they're still a good tool. They're just less reliable at changing your mood.

Another option: treat the limit screen as a cue to come back down. Phone face down, one long sigh, then in for 4 and out for 6, three rounds. About 30 seconds. Stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy.

We're building DeRot around this idea. It pauses your apps while you reset with a few calming breaths, and it's coming soon to iOS.

Read the full guide for the research and a step-by-step script.
